6.0.s.en: 1. Rashness in standing surety for others (irresponsible conduct)

6.0.0.en: My son, if thou be surety for thy friend, if thou hast stricken thy hand with a stranger, thou art snared with the words of thy mouth, thou art taken with the words of thy mouth. Do this now, my son, and deliver thyself, when thou art come into the hand of thy friend; go, humble thyself, and make sure thy friend.

6.0.1.en: Give not sleep to thine eyes, nor slumber to thine eyelids.

6.0.2.en: Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler." [1-5].

6.0.3.en: In the previous chapter the wise Solomon warned the young man against confusing pure love, which builds up the personality and supports the soul, with lust, which destroys the whole being of man: body, soul and spirit. Here he warns the young man against hasty, unwise love, in which a person stands surety for another without regard for counting the cost. The wise man warned against this conduct several times (Prov 11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26; 27:13). According to Jewish law, a surety who is unable to pay the debt of the one for whom he stood surety is liable to have his property confiscated, and even to be sold as a slave for the creditor's account.

6.0.4.en: A young man often comes forward as surety for another out of pride and self-confidence in himself and his means, without deliberation. Therefore the wise man asks him to be humble, to cast himself down, as it were, at the feet of the debtor and ask him to pay what he owes. He did not ask him to cast himself down at the feet of the creditor so that he might forgive the debt or postpone it for the debtor, but at the feet of the debtor so that he might pay what he owes. This shows that he is speaking of a pledge given for a merchant who is able to pay, not for a poor man who needs a loan out of necessity.

6.0.5.en: Some think that the practice of standing surety developed and increased among the Jews at that time, so that some wealthy young men specialized in conducting surety transactions between individuals of their own people and strangers, their aim being to take the greatest possible amount of interest. In this they were swept along by greed, but their lives ended in bankruptcy, indeed in utter ruin. So the warning here is not against humane action and generosity in giving surety, but against wrong commercial dealings.

6.0.6.en: The wise Solomon presents to us the following principles concerning standing surety for others:

6.0.7.en: First: do not be hasty in standing surety for another, for although this surety is given by a word of the mouth, the believer is bound by the word he utters. This haste is reckoned a snare in which a person falls. Some say that a man's lips are a snare in which he falls through his own words. Therefore it is fitting for the believer to devote his energies to controlling the tongue more than the other members, and to put a bridle on it. We need the work of the Holy Spirit, who sanctifies the tongue.

6.0.8.en: * An unbridled tongue is a dangerous snare, and needs a strong bridle. Therefore one of them said: "A man's lips are a strong snare set for him, catching him by the words of his mouth."

6.0.9.en: Let us control this member more than all the other members.

6.0.10.en: Let us bridle it, and keep away from it words of violent reproach, coarse and foolish expressions, a wounding manner, and the evil habit of swearing.

6.0.11.en: St. John Chrysostom * Much talking is a throne of vanity...

6.0.12.en: Much talking is a sign of ignorance.

6.0.13.en: * The friend of silence draws near to God, and as he converses with Him in secret he is enlightened by His light.

6.0.14.en: St. John Climacus Second: if you stand surety for a person, do not take the matter lightly, but it is fitting that you neither sleep nor rest, exerting every effort so that the debtor may pay the debt for which you stood surety. In this way you free yourself from the obligation, and you will be like the roe hastening from the hand of the hunter, or like the bird flying far from the snare.

6.0.15.en: It is observed that the words "hand" and "hunter" in Arabic, as in Hebrew, are "sayyad, yad"; and that the word "hand" is common to both words, since through his ignorance he falls captive into the hand of the hunter and does not escape from it.

6.0.16.en: Ben Sirach encourages the believer to treat his brother with love combined with wisdom, saying:

6.0.17.en: "A good man will be surety for his neighbor, and he who has lost all sense of shame will fail him...

6.0.18.en: Suretyship has ruined many men of means, and tossed them about like the waves of the sea.

6.0.19.en: It has driven powerful men into exile, so that they wandered among foreign nations.

6.0.20.en: The sinner who rushes into suretyship in pursuit of gain rushes into his own judgment.

6.0.21.en: Help your neighbor according to your ability, and take care for yourself lest you fall" (Sir 29:14-20).

6.0.22.en: Once again we affirm that the wise Solomon does not command us not to stand surety, but to act with wisdom, whatever the motive for it. There is a Jewish (rabbinic) proverb: "When the fool goes to the market, the merchants rejoice."

6.1.0.en: 6 Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise: 7 Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler, 8 Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest. 9 How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? 10 Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep: 11 So shall thy poverty come as one that travelleth, and thy want as an armed man.

6.1.1.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that man, who was created in the image and likeness of God, is brought low by sin until he descends to the point where animals and insects become better than he in many matters. The wild beasts, such as lions, when they gather together support one another, and none of them attacks the other; but man, when he gathers with his brother, often has a spirit of jealousy and envy arise between them, which sometimes drives them to commit murder. Man also loses his speech, his diligence and his wisdom, so that he needs to learn these from the ant. As the wise Solomon says:

6.1.3.en: Consider her ways, and be wise.

6.1.4.en: Which having no guide, overseer, or ruler,

6.1.5.en: Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.

6.1.6.en: How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard?

6.1.7.en: When wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?" (6-9)

6.1.8.en: The wise man asks the sluggard to go to the ant so that he may learn many things from it, among them:

6.1.9.en: A. Although there is no leader or general manager, the ants know how to work together for the good of the community (team work). The ants preceded man in organized, collective work, without struggle over positions of power or authority.

6.1.10.en: B. The ant does not need a leader to compel it to work, but works by an inner instinct without outside pressure, whereas man often works, not out of his inner faithfulness, but out of fear of others, lest he lose his wage or his dignity.

6.1.11.en: C. Ants prepare their food in the spring, the summer and the autumn, so that they may sleep and rest in the time of winter. They work as long as it is the time for work, and keep on working for long periods, so that when the time comes in which they cannot work they find beside them what they may eat. They do not know sleep in the times of work, but labor diligently without slackness. So it is fitting for us to work while it is day, so that when night falls we may rest.

6.1.12.en: Among the insects there is none so truly diligent and constantly working as the ant; even the bee, which gathers nectar from the flowers, is not as ever-moving and ever-working as the ant.

6.1.13.en: D. The wise Solomon did not mention the ant's care for its young: it carries the young one before its growth is complete and brings it out of the hole and places it at the entrance, to be exposed to the light of the sun and benefit from it. And when it senses that rain is coming, it carries it back inside the hole, and puts a very small stone so that water does not seep in to its young. Truly the ant is counted a wonderful and living example for man of tireless work together with care for the little ones.

6.1.14.en: Some in the early ages were ashamed to be taught by a woman, even if this woman was the mother, as St. Augustine confessed, saying to God: "You were speaking to me through my mother's mouth, but I was not listening to You, because You were speaking to me through the mouth of a woman." And St. John Chrysostom marvels at those who refuse to be taught by some women, such as mothers, while man has descended to the level at which he needs to learn from a small insect like the ant.

6.1.15.en: * If you are ashamed to have a woman as your teacher, flee from sin; then you will be able to ascend to the wisdom that God gives you. As long as you sin, the Holy Scripture sends you not only a woman but an irrational creature, and sometimes a lowly one! Truly it is not shameful that it sends you as a pupil to an ant, while you are honored with reason.

6.1.16.en: * We say: Notice how a being lower than you is full of zeal and watchfulness! Therefore receive from these insects (animals) the best counsel in work, and marvel at your Lord, not only because He created heaven and earth, but also because He created the ant. For although it is small, it offers proof of the greatness of God's wisdom. Look how the ant behaves with prudence, and how God planted in this small body a desire to work without ceasing!

6.1.17.en: St. John Chrysostom * Be prudent, imitate the ant as the Scripture says: "Let it be stored up in summer lest you hunger in winter."

6.1.18.en: Winter is the last day, the day of judgment.

6.1.19.en: Winter is the day of rebellion and bitterness.

6.1.20.en: Gather what will be yours in the future, or else you will perish because you are neither prudent nor wise.

6.1.21.en: St. Augustine St. John Cassian almost devoted a whole discourse to the necessity of work and not being idle, even for those living in solitude:

6.1.22.en: * (The Apostle Paul), like a skilled and experienced physician, tries to heal by performing surgery with a spiritual weapon, saying: "That ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us" (2 Thess 3:6). So he commands them to avoid those who devote no time to work, and to cut them off like members of the body disfigured by the sores of idleness and emptiness, lest the disease of slackness and laziness pass gradually to the healthy parts of the body, like some deadly contagious diseases.

6.1.23.en: When the Apostle speaks of those who do not work with their hands, and eat their bread in quietness, he urges us to avoid them. Listen to the kinds of blame and rebuke with which he assails them at the outset. First, he calls them "disorderly," and also, "not after the tradition." In other words, he describes them as stubborn because they do not walk according to his direction, and as unseemly because they do not keep the proper, fixed times in their going out, their visits and their conversations. For the person who is not orderly is certainly exposed to all these faults.

6.1.24.en: "And not after the tradition which he received of us": by this he rebukes them as being in some way rebellious and scoffers, who have made light of the teaching they received from him and did not take care of it, and did not follow what they remembered he had taught them not in word only but also by actually practicing it... "For yourselves know how ye ought to follow us" (2 Thess 3:7).

6.1.25.en: The Apostle piles up an enormous heap of reproach and blame when he affirms that they did not heed what still remained in their memory. And those who learned it not only by oral instruction, but also received it in his own person as an example in work which must be imitated.

6.2.0.en: 12 A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth. 13 He winketh with his eyes, he speaketh with his feet, he teacheth with his fingers; 14 Frowardness is in his heart, he deviseth mischief continually; he soweth discord. 15 Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly; suddenly shall he be broken without remedy.

6.2.1.en: If the sluggard is condemned for his laziness even though he practices no evil, how much more will be the condemnation of one who practices evil, especially baseness! For such a man does everything in an affected manner, plotting craftily against others; a man like this loses his innocence by withdrawing from the way of the Lord, and so destroys himself.

6.2.2.en: The wise man presents seven deeds marked by deceit, which the foolish man practices.

6.2.3.en: "A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth, he winketh with his eyes, he speaketh with his feet, he teacheth with his fingers.

6.2.7.en: Therefore shall his calamity come suddenly.

6.2.8.en: Suddenly shall he be broken without remedy" [12-15].

6.2.9.en: The word "base" in Hebrew means literally "a man of Belial," that is, the worthless man who is good for nothing, because his dealings are with false words.

6.2.10.en: The base man is marked by the following characteristics:

6.2.11.en: A. A wicked man: the Hebrew word means an apostate man, separated from God and opposing Him. He uses his mouth to pervert the truth, walking in crookedness.

6.2.12.en: B. He speaks not only with his tongue, but he presses into service, if possible, all the members of his body to express the crookedness, or deviation from the truth, that he carries within him. His mouth speaks crookedly, his eyes wink in mockery, his feet move to speak what accords with his corrupt heart, and his fingers point toward what he wishes to accomplish.

6.2.13.en: In the East the feet and the fingers are often used as a means of expressing certain thoughts, especially in the presence of persons from whom a man wishes to hide what he is communicating to another; so instead of speaking with the tongue he speaks by the movements of his feet and fingers, without those present realizing what the person means. Some merchants are also known to have done this when entering into the conclusion of deals in the presence of others: they sit on the ground and place a piece of cloth over their thighs, and express what they are saying through the movements of their fingers. In the same way the Brahmins convey religious secrets to their disciples while hiding their hands in the folds of their garments; thus they teach with their fingers. This was known among the ancient Romans, and the classical writers described it.

6.2.14.en: Some think that Simon Peter could not speak to the Lord Christ to ask who would betray Him, so he made a sign to Him, speaking with him in the language of gestures, for it is said: "Simon Peter therefore beckoned to him, that he should ask who it should be of whom he spake" (Jn 13:24).

6.2.15.en: Corrupt girls and dancers used to use their feet to express what they wished to say. Some think that the wise Solomon most likely meant these corrupt women when he spoke of the base and wicked man.

6.2.16.en: C. Frowardness is in his heart: if the outward members of his body are devoted to evil, the secret of this is the heart, which carries falsehoods instead of the truth.

6.2.17.en: Whoever carries the Lord Christ, the Truth Himself, in his heart, all the members of his body are sanctified; and whoever carries the devil, the liar and the father of liars, all the members of the body are used to practice his evil works and deceits.

6.2.18.en: * Purity of heart means purity of the eye with which we behold God, and without doubt our concern for purity of heart increases in proportion to the greatness of what we see with the heart.

6.2.19.en: St. Augustine * For the sake of purity of heart we ought to do everything and endure everything, and not cling to our relatives, our land (our possessions), our (earthly) honor, our position, the delights of the world and all kinds of pleasures...

6.2.20.en: We ought to do everything or seek anything for the sake of purity of heart. For its sake we seek solitude... and for its sake we fast and keep vigil and bear toils and nakedness and study, and acquire all the other virtues, so that we may prepare our hearts and keep them from all evil poisons, and thus ascend to the perfection of love...

6.2.21.en: So the things that come second in importance, such as fasting, vigil, renunciation of the world and meditation on the Holy Bible, these we must do looking to the chief goal, which is "purity of heart," which is "love." We must not lose this chief virtue because of fulfilling another virtue.

6.2.22.en: So if we do not carry out one of these other virtues for a compelling reason, no harm comes to us, so long as the chief virtue is present. It is not permissible for us to carry out a work that would cause us to lose this goal which we are discussing, but we strive for it whatever it may cost.

6.2.23.en: Abba Moses D. He devises evil without ceasing: he is not only deceived by the devil, but bears his mark, and urges all those around him to practice the works of the devil. Day and night, even in his dreams, he is occupied with practicing the works of his father, the devil.

6.2.24.en: E. He soweth discord: Father Gregory (the Great) says concerning the directions we should give to those who sow discord:

6.2.25.en: [There is a difference between the counsels given to the sowers of discord and to the makers of peace. The sowers of discord are advised to realize whom it is that they follow. It was said of the tares sown among the good wheat that an enemy did this (Mt 13:28), that is, a base angel... As the wise Solomon says, he is a base person, a man of no use, who walks with a froward mouth, and winks with his eyes, and stamps with his feet, and speaks with his finger, and devises evils without ceasing, with a heart in which are falsehoods, and sows discord.

6.2.26.en: Yes, the one about whom he wishes to speak is a sower of discord. He is called first base, because after the manner of the proud angel he first falls within himself by turning his thought away from the face of his Creator, and afterward sows discord outwardly. Rightly also is he described as winking with his eyes, speaking with his finger and stamping with his feet. For the watchfulness of the inner man keeps his outer members controlled in their order. Whoever loses the steadiness of his thought also falls outwardly into unseemly movements, and by his outward movements shows that he has no settled roots within. Let the sowers of discord hear what is written: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God" (Mt 5:9). And on the other side, let them realize that if the peacemakers are called children of God, those who oppose this (sowing discord) will certainly be called the sons of the devil.]

6.2.27.en: Truly the base or deceitful man sows discord even between husband and wife, to destroy the spirit of love and unity.

6.2.28.en: As for the end of the base man, it is to fall into sudden calamities; he is broken, and there is no healing for his breaking.

6.2.29.en: Perhaps he alludes here to the deceitful man who becomes deceived, especially by the sin of adultery, and so is suddenly exposed to stoning, according to the Mosaic Law, and his bones are broken, and there is no one to heal their breaking, or to have mercy on him as he is in the pit while stones rain down on his body from many.

6.3.s.en: 4. Seven things abominable to the Lord

6.3.0.en: 16 These six things doth the LORD hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him: 17 A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood, 18 An heart that deviseth wicked imaginations, feet that be swift in running to mischief, 19 A false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren.

6.3.1.en: The following statements describe the "man of Belial," and correspond to what was declared earlier in (verses 12-15), affirming that the gravest of sins is sowing discord among brothers.

6.3.2.en: "These six things doth the LORD hate: yea, seven are an abomination unto him.

6.3.3.en: A proud look, a lying tongue, and hands that shed innocent blood.

6.3.4.en: An heart that deviseth wicked imaginations, feet that be swift in running to mischief, a false witness that speaketh lies, and he that soweth discord among brethren" [16-19].

6.3.5.en: Some ask: "If God is love, does He bear hatred or aversion?" He is love, and by His love He hates hatred and aversion, and does not accept evil. In the book of Ecclesiastes He instructs us: "A time to love, and a time to hate" (Eccl 3:8). And in Deuteronomy it is said: "Neither shalt thou set thee up any image; which the LORD thy God hateth" (Deut 16:22). And in the Psalms: "Thou lovest righteousness, and hatest wickedness" (Ps 45:7), and in the book of Revelation: "But this thou hast, that thou hatest the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate" (Rev 2:6). Some compare God's fatherhood, which is full of love, to a father who loves his little child, but when he sees a poisonous snake wanting to kill him he hates it and kills it. So God, in His love for us, hates sin, which spreads its poisons in us.

6.3.6.en: The wise man presents to us a list of the things which the Lord hates. They are sins that cause above all harm to human life, as though whoever harms his brother wrongs God Himself, who desires the rest of mankind and seeks their peace and growth.

6.3.7.en: Let us look at this list not to condemn others, but to discover our own faults and repent of them in a spirit of humility, with prayer and supplication and avoiding every door to evil.

6.3.9.en: A. A proud look: these are the eyes of the proud, for a man exalts himself over his brothers instead of looking at them with looks of sympathy and tenderness and eagerness to give. This is the first of the things that God hates, and Satan fell into this sin (Isa 14:13, 14). And he does not cease to urge every person to claim divinity and not to trust in God, thinking he has no need of Him. Therefore the Lord says to Job: "Look on every one that is proud, and abase him; and tread down the wicked in their place" (Job 40:12). And David the prophet cries out: "LORD, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty: neither do I exercise myself in great matters, or in things too high for me" (Ps 131:1). And God says in Isaiah: "To this man will I look, even to him that is poor and of a contrite spirit, and trembleth at my word" (Isa 66:2).

6.3.10.en: * There is no fault that destroys and plunders all the virtues, and strips a man of all righteousness and holiness, like the evil of pride, which is like a dangerous plague that attacks the whole man, and is not content with destroying a part of him or one member, but destroys the whole body by its deadly effect. Pride strives to cast a man down by a destructive fall, and immediately shatters those who have reached the summit of the virtues.

6.3.11.en: With any other fault it is content to cause within a wound of limited extent; even if it resists some of the virtues, it is directed mainly against one virtue only and attacks it in particular.

6.3.12.en: To make my meaning clear: gluttony, the desires of the belly and delicious dishes destroy the virtue of chastity (self-control). Greed and covetousness stain or blemish purity or cleanness. And anger does away with patience. Therefore the man who is enslaved to one of these sins lacks some of the virtues... The person is simply deprived of one of the virtues when he yields or submits to the vice (or iniquity) that opposes it with its enticements, but he can preserve his other virtues. But when this vice once takes possession of a wretched soul, it is like some predatory (ravening) beasts that demolish the lofty citadel of virtue, and utterly destroy and demolish the city, so that the vices rise up together to demolish and throw into confusion the fortresses of holiness.

6.3.13.en: The yoke of slavery to pride is harsh and painful, and by its tearing cruelty it strips the soul and overcomes every power of virtue.

6.3.14.en: St. John Cassian B. A lying tongue: it cannot utter the truth, and bears no kindness or sincere gentleness toward the brothers. This is the second thing that the Lord hates. Lying is a mark of the enemy of good, the devil, who is marked by lying along with pride; his work is to spread this spirit among all men, so that David the prophet cried out, saying: "I said in my haste, All men are liars" (Ps 116:11), and he also cries out, saying: "Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips, and from a deceitful tongue" (Ps 120:2).

6.3.15.en: C. Hands that shed innocent blood: man also bears the spirit of treachery and betrayal, like Judas the traitor. This is the third thing that God hates, namely violence and injustice, and the enemy of good was called a murderer from the beginning.

6.3.16.en: D. A heart that deviseth wicked imaginations: the fourth thing that God hates is the thoughts of evil that come from the defiled heart. For it lays false foundations for untrue imaginations and builds much upon them, setting up a building of falsehoods with which it distorts the image of its brothers and drives them into injustice.

6.3.17.en: E. Feet that be swift in running to mischief help a man to commit iniquity out of covetousness. When the heart is corrupted it draws the whole body toward evil, and the feet hasten to practice it. As Isaiah the prophet says: "Their feet run to evil, and they make haste to shed innocent blood: their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity; wasting and destruction are in their paths. The way of peace they know not; and there is no judgment in their goings: they have made them crooked paths: whosoever goeth therein shall not know peace" (Isa 59:7, 8).

6.3.18.en: F. A false witness that speaketh lies causes injustice to fall upon the innocent. Sadly, this sin which God hates has become common today; how easy it is for someone to hire a false witness who speaks lies.

6.3.19.en: G. He that soweth discord among brethren, whether at the level of the individual, or of families, or of societies, and sometimes between nations. If the peacemakers are called children of God (Mt 5:9), then the sowers of discord are called children of the devil.

6.3.20.en: These seven sins which God hates are like a mirror into which a man looks and discovers his weakness; then he hastens to God, confessing his sins and asking Him to cleanse him.

6.4.0.en: 20 My son, keep thy father's commandment, and forsake not the law of thy mother: 21 Bind them continually upon thine heart, and tie them about thy neck. 22 When thou goest, it shall lead thee; when thou sleepest, it shall keep thee; and when thou awakest, it shall talk with thee. 23 For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light; and reproofs of instruction are the way of life.

6.4.1.en: The divine commandment supports the believer so that he does not fall into the preceding sins; therefore he must keep this commandment which his father teaches him, and store it in the depths of his heart and bind it to his whole being. As it is written in the book of Deuteronomy:

6.4.2.en: "And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up. And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thine hand, and they shall be as frontlets between thine eyes. And thou shalt write them upon the posts of thy house, and on thy gates" (Deut 6:6-9; cf. Deut 11:18-20).

6.4.3.en: "My son, keep thy father's commandment, and forsake not the law of thy mother.

6.4.4.en: Bind them continually upon thine heart.

6.4.6.en: When thou goest, it shall lead thee; when thou sleepest, it shall keep thee; and when thou awakest, it shall talk with thee" [20-22].

6.4.7.en: The wise man does not cease to remind his disciple to hear the commandments of his father and hold fast to the law of his mother (Prov 1:8), who present to him the word of God or the divine commandment.

6.4.8.en: What does the commandment offer him?

6.4.9.en: A. Inner satisfaction: he binds it continually upon his heart, and it satisfies all his feelings and emotions, and he does not suffer from inner emptiness.

6.4.10.en: B. True honor: it is an honor and glory to him, with which he encircles his neck as a sign of his kingship and of his sonship to God his heavenly Father. He writes it on the tablets of his heart or binds it to himself, and it regulates the center of his love, his feelings and his emotions, and all his thoughts, words and conduct come forth in harmony with the divine commandment.

6.4.11.en: C. A divine gift: here he personifies the law or commandment, presenting it as a teacher or trainer of the soul, a guardian of it and a friend; the commandment accompanies him as he walks the road of life, and guards him in his sleep, and converses with him in love, so that he feels neither isolation nor emptiness.

6.4.12.en: D. Heavenly guard: the true believer will not go to any place without seeking the guidance of the divine commandment. And he will not give sleep to his eyes unless he takes shelter under its wings. And when he awakes he enters with it into a conversation of love, through prayer and the study of the Holy Bible, and his whole being is filled with joy and satisfaction. He gives the firstfruits of his day, the early morning, to God, where he meets Him, speaking as a son with his father, and holds fast to the divine promises to plead for His heavenly mercies.

6.5.0.en: "For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light; and reproofs of instruction are the way of life" [23].

6.5.1.en: The commandment illumines our depths, so that we see the truth about ourselves and realize our constant need of the Savior. We also discover the work of the Holy Trinity in us and are filled with hope, and our eyes are opened to the knowledge of the divine will and the understanding of the divine mysteries. Thus we accept every discipline from the Lord and count it beneficial to our depths, for it draws us away from the pleasures of sins and their enticements to walk in the way of eternal life; it draws us away from the deceits of the evil one to receive divine truth and purity.

6.6.0.en: 24 To keep thee from the evil woman, from the flattery of the tongue of a strange woman. 25 Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids. 26 For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life. 27 Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned? 28 Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned? 29 So he that goeth in to his neighbour's wife; whosoever toucheth her shall not be innocent. 30 Men do not despise a thief, if he steal to satisfy his soul when he is hungry; 31 But if he be found, he shall restore sevenfold; he shall give all the substance of his house. 32 But whoso committeth adultery with a woman lacketh understanding: he that doeth it destroyeth his own soul. 33 A wound and dishonour shall he get; and his reproach shall not be wiped away.

6.6.1.en: He returns to the sin of adultery, of which the wise Solomon has often spoken, and which some call "the sin of the age." Strangely, many drink this sin like water, and count it a kind of love!

6.6.2.en: How many marriages, among the young or the old, have been destroyed by a third party, a man or a woman, who came in to rob the spouses of their unity.

6.6.3.en: "To keep thee from the evil woman, from the flattery of the tongue of a strange woman" [24].

6.6.4.en: By realizing the wisdom of God and accepting His disciplines we are kept from the sweet and deceitful tongue of the adulterous woman, so as to receive the firm words of God, which are full of truth.

6.6.5.en: The words of the evil woman carry desires mixed with poison, but the words of the Lord are love full of eternal life. Therefore we listen to the tongue of the Lord, not the tongue of wicked women.

6.7.0.en: "Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids" [25].

6.7.1.en: The wise Solomon presents to us his bitter experiences, for he fell into the snares of the beauty of women, and so turned aside to the worship of idols and shared in their abominations.

6.7.2.en: The care of women to beautify their eyes and the lashes of their eyelids so that the eyes appear wide and attractive is an ancient matter in the East.

6.7.3.en: It is not the beauty of a woman nor her care for her appearance that is the secret of man's fall, but the deviation of the heart. Therefore the wise man says: "Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life" (Prov 4:23). Sin begins in the heart, therefore he warns us: "Lust not after her beauty in thine heart."

6.7.4.en: * Do not let the desire for beauty overcome you. For many nets and snares are set by Satan. Looking at an adulteress is a snare set for the one who loves her. (The corruption of) our eyes is nets set for us, as it is written: "neither let her take thee with her eyelids." Therefore we set nets for ourselves, and we fall into them and are entangled. We bind ourselves with chains as it is written: "for every one is bound with the cords (ropes) of his sins."

6.7.5.en: St. Ambrose The blessed Clement of Alexandria wrote in his discourse "On Virgins":

6.7.6.en: * Therefore we do not permit any person whatever to sit (for long periods) with a married woman, and still more not to live in one house with a maiden who has offered her life as a vow, nor to sleep where she sleeps, nor to be her constant companion. For this is a thing that those who fear the Lord abhor and hate.

6.8.0.en: St. Clement of Rome "For by means of a whorish woman a man is brought to a piece of bread: and the adulteress will hunt for the precious life" [26].

6.8.1.en: In the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Syriac it reads: "For the hire of a harlot is a single loaf of bread." It is as though the man hires the harlot at a paltry price, a loaf of bread, but does not realize that she draws another price, his own precious soul. A person thinks that sin is very cheap and costs him nothing, while he loses his inner life and his eternal salvation.

6.8.2.en: "Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?

6.8.3.en: "Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned?

6.8.4.en: So he that goeth in to his neighbour's wife.

6.9.0.en: Whosoever toucheth her shall not be innocent" [27-29].

6.9.1.en: To be lax with the sin of adultery is to play with fire: his lust blazes up as a fire that burns his clothes so that he becomes naked in shame, and it scorches his feet so that he tastes bitterness and cannot complete the journey of his life as is fitting for him, and it also burns every longing for purity, so that he is not innocent in the eyes of God and men.

6.9.2.en: * Let us flee from (this fire of lust) although it follows us, not only running behind us but also within us. Let us take heed with all diligence lest, while we flee from it, we carry it within us. For we would rather only flee, but if we do not cast it completely out of our minds we have rather held on to it and not let it go.

6.10.0.en: Let us leap and pass over it, lest it be said to us: "Walk in the flame of your fire which you have kindled" (Isa 50:11). For just as one who takes fire into his bosom burns his clothes, so one who walks on burning coals must needs have his feet scorched, as it is written: "Can one go upon hot coals, and his feet not be burned?" [28].

6.10.1.en: St. Ambrose * Evil lust is like a flame and fire. Does fire burn a garment, and the lust of adultery not burn the soul?!

6.10.2.en: St. Augustine * If the eye falls upon a person, at least do not let the inner affection follow it. For looking is not a sin, but a man must be careful that it not become a source of sin.

6.10.3.en: Let the bodily eye look, and let the eye of the heart be closed, and let humility of mind remain.

6.10.4.en: We have a Lord who is strict and forbearing... The Lord says: "Whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart" (Mt 5:28). He did not say: "Everyone who looks commits adultery," but "whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her." He condemns the inner lust, not the glance.

6.10.5.en: St. Ambrose * Lest you say: What harm is there in the eyes, since the look is not necessarily corrupting? He shows you that lust is a fire and that the body is like a garment. The latter can be an easy prey, for lust is tyrannical. The harm does not occur within only, but extends and goes forth until it finds an outlet outside. For whoever looks at a woman, even if he flees from the temptation, is not completely pure from lust.

6.10.6.en: And why should a man remain in toil when it is in his power to avoid it and be freed from it? See what Job says: "I made a covenant with mine eyes not to think of another's wife." So he knows the danger of corruption. And for the same reason Paul subdued his body and brought it into bondage. And in a symbolic way, whoever allows an impure thought to dwell in his heart keeps a fire in his bosom. And whoever practices sin in deed walks on coals and destroys himself.

6.10.7.en: St. Hippolytus If a thief cannot justify himself before the law even if he stole in order to eat because he was hungry, what excuse is there for the adulterer who commits the sin and destroys his own soul?!

6.10.8.en: "Men do not despise a thief, if he steal to satisfy his soul when he is hungry.

6.10.9.en: But if he be found, he shall restore sevenfold; he shall give all the substance of his house.

6.10.10.en: But whoso committeth adultery with a woman lacketh understanding.

6.10.11.en: He that doeth it destroyeth his own soul.

6.11.0.en: A wound and dishonour shall he get; and his reproach shall not be wiped away" [30-33].

6.11.1.en: People pity the poor man who steals in order to eat, but the law does not acquit him; it requires him to restore sevenfold what he stole, and if he has not the means to pay, he is sold as a slave (Ex 22:1-4; Lev 25:39).

6.11.2.en: * The thief is a grave offender, but the adulterer is graver than he. For the former acts so for a pitiable reason, yet at the same time need constrains him to it, whereas the latter has no necessity constraining him; rather his madness makes him rush into the pit of iniquity.

6.12.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Whoever commits adultery with a married woman is exposed not only to shame but also to death [33]. Among the Romans, if a man was caught committing this act, the husband had the right to hold to the law and kill him, so that the adulterer is in disgrace and loses his life.

6.13.0.en: "For jealousy is the rage of a man: therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance.

6.13.1.en: He will not regard any ransom; neither will he rest content, though thou givest many gifts." [24-25].

6.13.2.en: Here he speaks of the jealousy of the husband whose wife the adulterer has violated; he takes vengeance for his dignity and honor, and does not ask for a ransom however great, but demands the death of the adulterer.

6.13.3.en: Let me act in the spirit of wisdom and love,
